The Assistant view in Gramps Web (if enabled in your installation) gives access to an AI assistant that answers questions about your family tree.

Warning

As with any AI assistant, answers can be wrong. Use the links in the answer to check the records it is based on.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The assistant doesn't know your tree in advance. To answer a question, a large language model looks up the records it needs, much as you would yourself:

  • it searches the tree with the full-text search,
  • it filters people, events, and families by criteria such as names, dates, places, or the number of children,
  • it finds ancestors, descendants, and other relatives of a person, with their relationship,
  • it reads complete records of people, families, events, places, and notes.

It then answers based on the records it has found, with links to them. While it is working, the tools it is using are shown, so you can follow along. Questions that take longer run in the background – you can navigate away and come back.

The assistant answers only from your tree, not from the general knowledge of the language model – even about well-known people. If the tree does not record something, it says so, mentioning related information it found, for example in a note. It only sees what you are allowed to see: links to private records are shown as plain text for users who can't view them.

Follow-up questions keep the context of earlier questions in the same conversation, so you can ask "And when did he die?" after asking about a person.

docs.title: What you can ask
docs.text:
• Facts about people: "When was Mary Smith born?" or "What are the names of John Doe's children?"
  • Relatives: "Who are the grandparents of Jane Smith?" or "Which descendants of Johann Meyer emigrated to America?"
  • Searches with criteria: "Who was born in London after 1850?", "List marriages between 1920 and 1950", or "Which couples had five or more children?"
  • Places: "Which events happened in Paris?" or "Who was born in Denmark?" – places within a larger place are included.
  • Notes: "What do the notes say about the farm of the Meyer family?"

Questions that need the whole tree at once, such as "What is the most common first name?", work less well, since the assistant only sees a limited number of records per lookup.

docs.title: Asking about images
docs.text:
If the server administrator has enabled it, the prompt has a button to attach images. You can also paste an image or drop image files onto the prompt. Up to four images can be attached to a question, for example a scan of a church record to ask "Who is mentioned in this entry, and are they in my tree?"

The images are only sent with the question they are attached to. Follow-up questions can refer to what the assistant said about them, but not to the images themselves, so attach them again if needed. If your tree has a limit on AI usage, each image counts like an additional question.

docs.title: Letting the assistant change your tree
docs.text:
If the server administrator has enabled it, editors, owners, and administrators can ask the assistant to change the tree, for example "Add a baptism on 3 May 1802 in St. Mary's to Johann Meyer" or "Fix the birth year of Anna Smith, it should be 1871".

The assistant never changes anything on its own. It answers with a Proposed changes card that lists every record it would add, edit, or delete, with the old values struck through and the new values highlighted. Nothing happens until you click Apply. The changes are then made in one step, which you can undo like any other edit, from the message that appears or in the revision history.

Check a proposal carefully before applying it – in particular that the assistant picked the right person, and that it didn't add a new record (such as a place or source) that already exists in your tree under a slightly different name. If a proposal is not quite right, say what to change, and the assistant proposes again.

Once a proposal has been applied, older proposals in the same conversation can no longer be applied, since they were made for the tree as it was before. The same happens if one of the affected records has been changed in the meantime.

docs.title: Tips for asking questions
docs.text:
• Name the people. The assistant doesn't know who you are or who your home person is, so instead of "my grandmother", ask about "the grandmother of Anna Smith (born 1950)". You can also use Gramps IDs, e.g. "the children of I0042".
  • Be specific when names are common: "When did the John Smith born in 1850 in Boston marry?" is better than "When did John Smith marry?"
  • Use your language. You can ask in your own language and receive answers in the same language.
  • Ask again differently if an answer looks incomplete – for example by naming the place or time period you are interested in.

Tip

Please share your experience about things that work and don't work with the community.

docs.title: Chromosome Browser
docs.text:
The chromosome browser is a tool to visualize a person's DNA matches. It shows the DNA segments shared with other people in the tree as colored bars on the chromosomes.

You can find it under the “Chromosome Browser” tab in the DNA view.

For each chromosome, the upper (light blue) bar represents the copy inherited from the father, the lower (light red) bar the one inherited from the mother. The shared segments are shown as colored bars on top of these. Segments whose side (paternal or maternal) is not known are shown in a separate track between the two. Where segments of several matches overlap, they are drawn in separate, thinner lanes, so that every segment stays visible.

Clicking on the name of a match in the legend, only this person's shared segments are shown.

docs.title: Grouping by common ancestors
docs.text:
Above the legend, you can switch between coloring the segments by Matches and by Common ancestors. With common ancestors, matches who descend from the same most recent common ancestors with the selected person share a color and a row in the legend. This shows at a glance which parts of the chromosomes were inherited from which ancestral couple – a segment of another match that overlaps with those of a group on the same side probably comes from the same ancestors, which helps to place a new, unknown match.

The groups are ordered by the closest relationship first. Matches without known common ancestors are grouped under "Unknown". A match who is related through several lines is grouped by the closest one.

docs.title: Saving the chart
docs.text: To save the chart, click the download button next to the person selector. It downloads an SVG file with a white background and the legend, including each match's total shared centimorgans. If a match or group is selected in the legend, only that one is included.

docs.title: How Gramps organizes data
docs.text:
Gramps Web stores a family tree not as a chart, but as separate objects – people, families, events, places, sources, and so on – that are linked to each other. Once you know how these objects fit together, entering data becomes predictable: anything you want to link to has to exist first.

Gramps Web uses the same data model as Gramps Desktop, so everything on this page applies to both.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Object What it represents Examples Person An individual You, your grandmother Family A couple, their children, or both Your parents and their children Event Something that happened, with a date and a place Birth, marriage, census, emigration Place A geographic location A village, a parish, a country Source A document or collection of information A parish register, a census, a book Citation A specific reference within a source Page 12, entry 3 of the parish register Repository Where a source is kept An archive, a library, a website Note Free text A transcription, research remarks Media object A file A photo, a scanned certificate

Every object type has its own list in Gramps Web, see Lists.

docs.title: People and families
docs.text:
Parents and children are not linked to each other directly, but through a family. A family has up to two partners and any number of children:

  • Your parents and you are linked through the family in which you are a child.
  • Your siblings are the other children of the same family.
  • You and your spouse form another family, in which you are a partner, together with your children.

A person can be a child in one family and a partner in several. Each child has a relationship to each of the parents, such as birth, adoption, or stepchild, and each family has a relationship type, such as married or civil union.

This is why "adding parents" to a person means adding the person as a child to a family – which the tree chart does for you in one step.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
A birth, death, or marriage is not a field of a person, but an event of its own, with a type, a date, a place, and a description. People are linked to an event with a role: the person whose birth it is has the role "Primary", while someone else might be linked to the same event as a witness.

Events that concern a couple, such as a marriage, belong to the family rather than to either partner. An event can also be shared by several people – for example a census record listing a whole household – instead of being entered once per person.

This affects editing. The event itself – its type, date, place, and description – is the same for everybody linked to it, so editing a shared event from one person's page changes it for all of them. The edit dialog therefore lists the other participants first, and the fields only become editable after Edit for everyone. What belongs to one person's link to the event – the role, and citations, notes, and attributes that only apply to that person – is edited on the event's page, in the Participants tab in edit mode. There you can also add and remove participants. For example, a godparent's role and the note "signed with a mark" belong to the godparent's link to the baptism, not to the baptism itself.

docs.title: Shared objects: places and sources
docs.text:
Places, sources, citations, repositories, notes, and media objects exist in their own right, and any number of other objects can refer to the same one. This has a few consequences:

  • Create once, select many times. The village where ten of your ancestors were born is one place, selected in ten birth events. If you correct its name or coordinates, the correction applies everywhere.
  • Create it before you select it. Forms in Gramps Web select places and sources that already exist. Create a new place or source first using the + (Add) button in the top app bar.
  • Places are nested. A place can be enclosed by a larger one – a village by a county, the county by a country – so you don't have to repeat the whole hierarchy for every village.
  • Sources and citations are separate. A source is the parish register as a whole; a citation is the specific entry that supports a fact, with its page, date, and your confidence in it. Many citations can point to the same source.

If you have accidentally created the same place or source twice, you can merge the duplicates.

docs.title: Editing an object's page
docs.text:
On the page of a source, repository, or media object, click the title in edit mode to change it (for a media object, its description). Press Enter, click ✓, or click elsewhere to save; press Escape or click ✕ to cancel.

Most lists on an object's page keep the order you give them, for example the events, names, attributes, addresses, citations, or the children of a family. In edit mode, select a row and move it with the up and down buttons, or drag it to its new position: with the mouse, press the row and move it; on a touch screen, press and hold the row until it is picked up. Press Escape while dragging to cancel. Media in the gallery can be reordered the same way, see Profile pictures.

docs.title: The Home Person
docs.text:
The Home Person is the person the family tree charts start from and the default starting point for reports. See First login for how to set it.

Different from Gramps Desktop

In Gramps Desktop, the Home Person is stored in the family tree database, so it is the same for everyone who opens that database. Gramps Web does not use it. Instead, the Home Person is stored in your browser, separately for each tree: it is not shared with other users, and it does not follow you to a different browser or device. After importing a tree from Gramps Desktop, or when you use Gramps Web on another device, you have to set it again.

docs.title: A recommended order
docs.text:
When entering a new family by hand, this order avoids jumping back and forth between forms:

  1. Places and sources. Create the places you need and, if you record sources, the source you are working from.
  2. People. Add the people with their birth and death dates and places. This is fastest in the edit mode of the Family Tree chart, which creates the families for you – see Start a new tree and Editing the family tree.
  3. Further events. Open a family (for example from a person's Relationships tab) to add the marriage, and a person's page to add other events.
  4. Citations. On the Source Citations tab of the person, event, or other object that a source supports, add a new citation, select the source, and enter the page.
  5. Notes and media. Attach transcriptions, photos, and scans – see Add media files.

docs.title: Entering dates
docs.text:
A date is entered as separate year, month, and day fields, which can also be filled in using a date picker. Leave out the parts you don't know: a year alone is a valid date. Instead of guessing an exact day, describe what you actually know by choosing the date's type with the chips above the fields. A hint below the chips explains the selected type:

What you know Type Example The exact date, or part of it Regular 12 March 1850, or just 1850 An approximate date About about 1850 A limit Before, After before 1900 The date lies somewhere within a period Range between 1850 and 1855 (fields "Earliest" and "Latest") Something lasted for a period Span from 1850 to 1855

For a Span, either of the two dates ("From" and "To") can be left empty, so "from 1850" or "to 1855" is a Span with only one date.

The Quality and Calendar fields are under More options, which opens by itself when a date uses either of them. The quality records how you arrived at a date: "Estimated" for an educated guess, "Calculated" for a date derived from other information, such as a birth year calculated from an age at death.

About and estimated dates cover 50 years either way

When Gramps compares dates, it treats a date of the type "about" – and any date with the quality "Estimated" – as a range reaching from 50 years before to 50 years after the given date. For example, filtering the People list for people born between 1840 and 1860 also finds a person born "about 1880", because that date is taken to cover 1830 to 1930. In the same way, "before" and "after" are taken to reach up to 50 years before or after the date.

This can lead to surprising results, so use "about" and "Estimated" only when you can't narrow the date down. If you know a shorter period, a Range such as "between 1878 and 1882" is more precise.

The calendar lets you enter a date in the calendar used in the original record, such as the Julian calendar, instead of converting it yourself.

docs.title: Working with DNA matches
docs.text:
DNA matches are segments of DNA that agree between two individuals, identified by the presence of markers, so-called SNPs (the acronym for single nucleotide polymorphisms, pronounced “snips”).

To obtain this data, you need access to a DNA test that is uploaded to a matching database that allows to view DNA segment match data (e.g. MyHeritage, Gedmatch, FamilytreeDNA). Gramps Web does not perform the matching itself, as it only has access to the data you upload.

docs.title: Entering DNA match data
docs.text:
To enter DNA match data, you need edit permissions as the data is stored as a note in the Gramps database. The DNA view, accessible from the main menu, provides a convenient way to enter this data in the right format.

To enter a new match, click on the + button in the lower right. In the dialog that opens, select the two individuals. Note that the “First person” and the “Second person” are treated differently: the match is stored as an association from the first to the second person. Only the first person will be selectable for the DNA match view and chromosome browser. Typically, the first person is the one whose DNA test you have access to and the second person is a more distant relative.

If the second person is not in the database, you need to create it first by using the “Create person” button in the top right corner of the user interface. Once you have created the person, you can return to the DNA match view and select the newly created person.

Next, paste the raw data into the text field. The data should be a comma or tab separated table of matches, typically containing the chromosome number, the start and end position of the match, the number of SNPs in the match and the lenght of the match in units of centimorgans (cM). You can also drag and drop a file with the match data into the text field.

A minimal example of such a table is:

Chromosome,Start Location,End Location,Centimorgans,SNPs
6,6358001,18115715,19.6,7424
7,150135758,154205894,10.9,2816

If the format is valid, a preview is shown below the text field as a table.

Finally, click on the “Save” button to store the match in the database.

docs.title: Viewing DNA match data
docs.text:
The DNA match view has a dropdown that allows to select each person in the database that has an associated DNA match. Once a person is selected, their matches are listed in a table: the name of the match, their relationship to the selected person, the total length of shared DNA in centimorgans (cM), the number of shared segments, and the length of the largest of these segments.

For matches that are already placed in the tree, the relationship column shows the relationship recorded in the tree (automatically determined from the Gramps database). For matches who are not related to the selected person in the tree, it shows the relationship estimated from the shared DNA, marked with "≈".

Clicking a match opens its page, with a summary of the shared DNA, the relationship estimate, a chart of the relationship in the tree, and the list of segments. Each segment shows whether it is on the paternal or maternal side. The side can either be entered manually (by providing a P for paternal or M for maternal in a column named Side in the raw data) or determined automatically from the most recent common ancestor. The download button next to the segments saves them as a CSV file in the format the match dialog accepts.

docs.title: Relationship estimate
docs.text:
Shared DNA is not proof of a specific relationship: the amount of DNA two relatives share varies a lot, and different relationships overlap. Gramps Web therefore shows a range of possible relationships with their probabilities, computed from the number and lengths of the shared segments (requires Gramps Web API 3.26 or newer).

Relationships are grouped by their degree:

  • Parent or child and Full sibling are shown on their own.
  • Relative of degree 2 includes half siblings, grandparents and grandchildren, and aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews.
  • Relative of degree 3 includes first cousins, great-grandparents, great-aunts and great-uncles, and half aunts and uncles.
  • Each further degree is about one generation further apart, e.g. first cousins once removed are degree 4 and second cousins are degree 5. Degree 9 and beyond are grouped as "9+".

Relationships with the same degree share about the same amount of DNA on average, so DNA alone cannot tell them apart. Use the ages of the people to decide between them – a 30-year-old relative of degree 2 of a 60-year-old is more likely a niece than a grandparent.

The estimate is most reliable for close relatives. For distant relationships, matches share only few segments, and the probabilities spread over several degrees.

docs.title: Checking the tree against the DNA
docs.text:
If the match is placed in the tree, Gramps Web checks whether the shared DNA fits the relationship recorded there. If the DNA is very unlikely for that relationship, a warning icon is shown in the matches table and a warning on the match page. The number in brackets, e.g. "1 : 500", compares how likely the DNA is for the recorded relationship with how likely it is for the most likely relationship.

A warning is a reason to look more closely, not proof of an error. Common causes are:

  • a mistake in the tree, such as a wrong parent,
  • a misattributed parentage, e.g. an unknown adoption or a different biological father,
  • incomplete match data, for example if only segments above a high threshold were copied from the testing service,
  • relationships through more than one line, e.g. people related through both their mother and father ("pedigree collapse"), which share more DNA than expected.

Relationships that are not by birth, such as through an adoption, are not checked.

docs.title: Editing a match
docs.text: To edit a match, open its page and click the edit button, or press e. Note that you can change the raw data, but not the individuals associated with the match – you need to delete the match and create a new one if you want to change the individuals.

docs.title: Private matches
docs.text: The dialogs for adding and editing a match have a Private switch. A private match, including its segments, is hidden from users who can't view private records. Private matches are marked with a lock for everybody else. See Private records for more about privacy.

docs.title: Working with match data in Gramps Desktop
docs.text:
The DNA match data is stored as a note in the Gramps database. The format is compatible with the DNA Segment Map Addon available for Gramps Desktop. Its wiki page contains more details about how to obtain the data, how to interpret it, and how to enter the data in Gramps.

Info

Gramps Web API v2.8.0 introduced some changes to the accept a broader range of raw DNA match data, which is not yet available in the Gramps Desktop Addon. The Gramps Desktop Addon will be updated in the future to support the same formats as well.

docs.title: Using Gramps Web for DNA genealogy
docs.text:
There are three branches of DNA genealogy dependending on the type of DNA used:

  • Autosomal chromosomes (numbered 1–22) are inherited from father and mother, so the probability of inheriting a piece of DNA from a given ancestor reduces exponentially with the number of generations. This makes them useful for finding degrees of separation with relatives when there is a relatively recent (few generations) common ancestor.
  • The Y chromosome is only passed on from father to son, so it can be used to trace the paternal lineage.
  • Mitochondrial DNA is passed on from mother to daughter, so it can be used to trace the maternal lineage.

At present, Gramps Web provides tools to work with matches from autosomal DNA tests. To obtain this data, you need access to a DNA test that is uploaded to a matching database that allows to view DNA segment match data (e.g. MyHeritage, Gedmatch, FamilytreeDNA). Gramps Web does not perform the matching itself, as it only has access to the data you upload.

docs.title: External Search
docs.text: Gramps Web allows you to search for people on external genealogy websites directly from a person's detail page.

docs.title: Performing an external search
docs.text:
To search for a person on external websites:

  1. Open the detail view of a person.
  2. Click the external search button.
  3. A popup will appear with links to various genealogy websites, such as CompGen, FamilySearch, and Ancestry.
  4. Clicking on a link will open the search results page on that website, pre-filled with the person's name, birth/death places, and other relevant information.

docs.title: Customizing external search options
docs.text:
You can customize which external search websites are displayed in the popup.

  1. In the external search popup, click the gear button at the top to enter edit mode.
  2. Select or deselect the websites you want to show or hide.
  3. Save your changes.

docs.title: Adding a custom search engine
docs.text:
You can add new external search websites with custom parameters.

  1. In the external search popup, click the gear button at the top to enter edit mode.
  2. Click the "+ Add custom search engine" button.
  3. A section will appear with fields for "Name" and "Search URL". Enter the website name and the URL with searchable parameters, such as https://example.com/search?name={{name_given}}_{{name_surname}}&place={{birth_place}}.
  4. Click the "Add" button to include the new search engine in the list.
  5. The new search engine will be saved and can be customized later.

docs.title: First login
docs.text:
When logging in to Gramps Web for the first time, a Preferences form (labeled User Settings) will be displayed requiring the user to select a language for the frontend and a Home Person. The Home Person selection can also be changed from the Home Page of the website.

The Home Person for a user of a Gramps Web website does not have to be the same person that the site's owner chose in Gramps for Desktops – it is a personal setting that can be different for every user of Gramps Web. The home person is used for the initial view of the family tree and the starting point for most Reports. A typical choice would be for a user to select themselves as Home Person. When collaborating with another member of a Tree, those users might want to set the common ancestor as the Home Person. This ensures a common point of reference for the distant relationships.

To select a person as Home Person, start typing a Given or Family Name in the text field and a drop-down list with matches will appear.

If the tree is still empty, there is nobody to choose yet. In this case, the home page shows a Get started card that guides editors through the first steps: first adding a person (or importing a family tree file), then connecting people by adding a family. The first person you create in an empty tree automatically becomes your Home Person. See Start a new tree for a step-by-step walkthrough.

The language and Home Person settings are stored in the browser's local storage, so they will persist on a given device. The Home Person is stored separately for each tree.

docs.title: Filter using the Gramps Object Query Language
docs.text:
The object list views (people, families, events, ...) and the task list have a filter field for expressions in the Gramps Object Query Language (GOQL).

To use it, open the filter panel, type an expression in the GOQL field and press Enter (or click Apply). The list is filtered by the expression, on top of any other active filters. If the expression is invalid, the field is marked as an error.

The expression always applies to the objects of the list you are in: in the People list, surname == 'Smith' finds the people with the surname Smith.

Note

The GOQL field needs Gramps Web API 3.24 or newer.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: A GOQL expression looks like a condition in the Python programming language. You don't need to know Python to use it – the examples below cover most needs.

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
A comparison has the form field operator value, for example surname == 'Smith'.

Operator Meaning == is equal to != is not equal to <, <= is less than, less than or equal to (earlier, smaller) >, >= is greater than, greater than or equal to (later, bigger) in [ ... ] is one of the listed values, e.g. surname in ['Meyer', 'Maier'] not in [ ... ] is none of the listed values 'text' in field the field contains the text, e.g. 'mill' in surname is None the field is empty or does not exist, e.g. death.date.sortval is None

Text goes in single or double quotes ('Smith'), numbers don't (1850). Comparisons can be chained, e.g. Date('1850') <= birth.date.sortval < Date('1900').

docs.title: Combining conditions
docs.text:
Conditions can be combined with and and or, and inverted with not. and takes precedence over or; use parentheses to group conditions:

(gender == Person.MALE and surname == 'Smith') or given_name == 'Mary'

docs.title: Text patterns
docs.text:
• like(field, 'pattern') matches a pattern in which % stands for any text and _ for a single character, e.g. like(given_name, 'J%') for all given names starting with "J".
  • regex(field, 'pattern') matches a regular expression, e.g. regex(surname, '^M[ae][iy]er$').

like and 'text' in field ignore upper and lower case (on SQLite, this only applies to the letters A–Z without accents). regex is case-sensitive.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
A field is the name of a property of the object, like gender or gramps_id, or a path to a nested property, like primary_name.first_name or primary_name.surname_list[0].surname. The square brackets select an element of a list by its position, starting from 0. The available properties are those of the Gramps data model. If a field does not exist, the error message lists the fields that do.

A few shortcuts are available:

  • People have given_name and surname, the given name and surname of the primary name.
  • People have birth and death, their birth and death events, e.g. birth.date.sortval or death.place.name.value.
  • Families have father and mother, e.g. father.surname == 'Smith'.
  • Events have place, citations have source, and places have enclosed_by, the enclosing place.

These can be chained, e.g. father.birth.place.name.value in the Families list. Two fields can also be compared with each other, e.g. father.surname == mother.surname.

docs.title: Lists of related objects
docs.text:
any(collection, condition) matches if at least one item of a collection meets the condition, and len(collection) counts the items. Without a condition, any(collection) matches if the collection is not empty. Collections are:

  • on almost every object: notes, citations, media, and tags
  • on people: events, families (as a partner), parent_families (as a child), and associations
  • on families: children
  • on all objects: backlinks, the objects that refer to it, which can be tested for their type with _class, e.g. any(backlinks, _class == 'Person')

any and len also work for lists stored in the object itself, such as alternate_names or primary_name.surname_list.

docs.title: Constants and types
docs.text:
Fixed values of Gramps are available as constants, such as Person.MALE, Person.FEMALE, Person.UNKNOWN, or the confidence levels Citation.CONF_VERY_LOW to Citation.CONF_VERY_HIGH. Types are compared by their value with constants such as EventType.BIRTH, FamilyRelType.MARRIED, NameType.BIRTH, PlaceType.VILLAGE, or RepositoryType.ARCHIVE:

type.value == EventType.BAPTISM

Custom types that you have entered yourself have no constant of their own.

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
Date('...') turns a date written as text into a value that can be compared with the sortval of a date, e.g. birth.date.sortval < Date('1800').

The sortval is a single point in time and ignores the type and quality of a date: "before 1800", "about 1800" and "1800" all have the same sortval, and for a range or span it is the start. To take these into account, compare the modifier or quality of the date with constants such as Date.MOD_ABOUT, Date.MOD_BEFORE, Date.MOD_AFTER, Date.MOD_RANGE, Date.MOD_SPAN, or Date.QUAL_ESTIMATED:

date.modifier == Date.MOD_ABOUT

docs.title: Commented examples
docs.text:
People list:

gender == Person.FEMALE and like(given_name, 'Mar%')

Women whose given name starts with "Mar".

Date('1850') <= birth.date.sortval < Date('1900')

People born from 1850 to 1899.

birth.place.name.value == death.place.name.value

People who were born and died in a place with the same name.

not any(notes)

People without notes.

any(events, type.value == EventType.BURIAL)

People with a burial event.

any(alternate_names, surname_list[0].surname == 'Meyer')

People with an alternate name with the surname Meyer.

Families list:

len(children) > 10

Families with more than 10 children.

len(children, gender == Person.FEMALE) == 3

Families with three daughters.

mother.death.date.sortval < father.death.date.sortval

Families in which the mother died before the father.

Events list:

type.value == EventType.BAPTISM and place.name.value == 'Berlin'

Baptisms in a place named Berlin.

Citations list:

confidence >= Citation.CONF_HIGH

Citations with a high or very high confidence.

Notes list:

'David' in text.string and private == True

Private notes that contain "David".

not any(backlinks)

Notes that are not attached to any object.

docs.title: Full reference
docs.text: For the full language reference, see the GOQL documentation.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text: Every object type in Gramps Web has a list view: People, Families, Events, Places, Sources, Citations, Repositories, Notes, and Media. They all work the same way and share the same tools for sorting, filtering, and editing in bulk.

docs.title: Sorting and paging
docs.text:
Click a column header to sort by that column; click it again to reverse the order. Sorting is performed by the server, so it applies to the whole list, not just the page you are looking at.

Long lists are split into pages. Use the pagination controls at the bottom to move between them.

On narrow screens the table automatically switches to a compact layout, so list views remain usable on a phone.

docs.title: Choosing columns
docs.text:
Click the gear icon at the right end of the toolbar above the list to open the Columns dialog. Tick or untick a column to show or hide it. Reset restores the default selection for that list.

At least one column must remain visible, so the last remaining column cannot be unticked.

Besides the default columns, every list offers a Tags column and, for users who can view private records, a Privacy column that shows a lock for each private object. If you have changed the column selection of a list before, new columns such as Tags are not added automatically; tick them in the dialog.

Your column selection is remembered per object type and per family tree. It is stored in your browser, so it is not visible to other users – but it also does not follow you to a different browser or device.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Click the filter button to open the filter panel. It offers three ways to filter, which can be combined:

  • Ready-made filters in collapsible sections that depend on the object type. For people, for instance, you can filter by name, birth year, death year, various person properties, the number of associations, tags, and whether an object is private or public. Families can be filtered by the name of the father, mother, or a child, sources by author, and places and repositories by their type.
  • Advanced filter – a condition builder for filters the ready-made ones can't express, described below.
  • GOQL – a text field for an expression in the Gramps Object Query Language, with syntax highlighting. Type the expression and press Enter or click Apply. If the expression is invalid, the field is marked as an error. An expression applies on top of the other filters.

Active filters are shown as chips in a row below the toolbar. Remove a single filter by clicking the chip's clear button, or use Clear all filters to remove them all at once.

docs.title: Advanced filter
docs.text:
Click Advanced filter at the bottom of the filter panel to open the condition builder. Its conditions are the filter rules known from Gramps Desktop, such as "People with the <name>" or "Ancestors of <person>".

  • Click Add condition to pick a rule. The rules are grouped into categories and can be searched by name or description.
  • Fill in the rule's parameters. Each parameter has a matching input, for example a date field, a tag selector, or an object selector for a person or place.
  • Choose how the conditions of a group are combined: All conditions, Any condition, or – via the menu next to them – Exactly one condition.
  • Click Add group to add a group of conditions inside another group, with its own way of combining them.
  • Select Not on a condition or group to invert it.

Click Apply to filter the list.

The ready-made filters and the GOQL expression that are active when you open the builder appear there as conditions. A GOQL expression can also be added as a condition of its own, for example to combine several expressions with Any condition. If the filter you build can be expressed with the ready-made filters, it is shown with them after applying. Otherwise, it is shown as a single Advanced filter chip, and the filter panel offers an Edit button to reopen the builder.

Note

Rules that refer to custom filters saved in Gramps Desktop are not available in the builder. The rules are shown in your language with Gramps Web API 3.24 or newer.

docs.title: Saved filters
docs.text:
To reuse a filter you have built, click Save in the condition builder and give it a name. Saving under an existing name replaces that filter. Saved filters in the builder lists the saved filters for the current object type; picking one loads it into the builder, where you can change it before clicking Apply.

Saved filters are stored in your browser, per family tree and object type, so they are not available to other users or on your other devices.

A saved filter can stop working when the tree changes, for example if it refers to a person who has since been deleted (the object selector then shows "Not found"). Such a filter cannot be applied or saved until the condition is fixed.

docs.title: Selecting objects and acting on them in bulk
docs.text:
Users with edit permissions see a Select button next to the filter button. Click it to enter selection mode, which adds a checkbox to every row.

Tick the objects you want, and a toolbar appears showing how many are selected, along with an Action dropdown and an Apply button.

The checkbox in the table header selects all objects on the current page. If more objects match the current filters, the toolbar then offers Select All (N), which selects all N matching objects across all pages. Unticking a row, changing the page or the filters, or leaving selection mode ends this selection.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
Select one or more objects, choose Delete, and click Apply. A confirmation dialog asks you to confirm, warning that the action cannot be undone.

Deleting more than ten objects runs as a background task. Its progress is shown next to the Apply button and in Notifications, and the list reloads when it is done.

Tip

Deletions are recorded in the revision history like any other change, so a mistaken bulk delete can be reversed by undoing the corresponding transaction.

docs.title: Tags and privacy
docs.text:
The actions Add Tag, Remove Tag, and Privacy change all selected objects at once (requires Gramps Web API 3.26 or newer):

  • Add Tag adds an existing tag or a new one you create in the dialog.
  • Remove Tag removes a tag from the selected objects that have it.
  • Privacy marks the selected objects as private or public. This only changes the objects themselves, not their parts or the records they link to – see Private records.

As with deleting, editing more than ten objects runs as a background task. The changes are recorded in the revision history as one transaction, so they can be undone together.

docs.title: Merge
docs.text:
Select exactly two objects, choose Merge, and click Apply. A dialog asks which of the two should provide the primary data for the merged object; click the one you want to keep as primary. The other object's data is merged into it and references are updated.

Merging is available for people, families, events, places, sources, and citations. It is not available for repositories, notes, and media objects.

In the media view, selection works in both the gallery and the list layout: in selection mode, clicking a tile or row toggles it. Media objects cannot be merged.

If you choose an action without a valid selection – for example a merge with only one object selected – a dialog explains what is required.

docs.title: Map
docs.text: The Map page displays all places in your family tree as interactive markers on a geographic map. It is accessible from the sidebar.

docs.title: Place markers
docs.text:
Only places that have GPS coordinates stored in the Gramps database are shown on the map. Places without coordinates are silently omitted. GPS coordinates can be set on the place detail page (edit the place and fill in the latitude and longitude fields).

Tip

If many of your places are missing from the map, open a place detail page and check whether latitude and longitude are set. You can add or correct coordinates directly from the place's edit view.

Each place with coordinates is shown as a marker. Clicking a marker opens a summary card showing the place name and its linked events and people. Click the place name in the card to open the full place detail page.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
The search box in the top-left corner of the map searches as you type and groups the results under three headings:

  • Places – places in your family tree. Selecting one pans the map to it and highlights its marker.
  • People – people in your family tree. Selecting one switches the map into the person view described below.
  • External – locations from OpenStreetMap, for anywhere in the world. Selecting one simply pans and zooms the map to that location; it does not filter or change your tree's places.

The external results are also useful when adding coordinates to a place: you can look the location up here to see where it is before entering its latitude and longitude.

docs.title: Following a person across the map
docs.text:
Selecting a person – from the map's search box, or with the Open in map button on a person's detail page – shows the places connected to that person's events – including the events of their families, such as marriages – joined by lines in chronological order. Small arrows along each line indicate the direction of travel, so you can follow a person's life from birth through to death across the map.

Places on a place detail page have an Open in map button as well, which opens the map centred on that place.

docs.title: Time slider
docs.text:
The time slider at the bottom of the page filters which place markers are shown based on the year of their associated events:

  • Drag the handle to select a year.
  • Only places linked to events that fall within the selected time window are shown.
  • Use this to trace where your ancestors lived at a particular point in history.

docs.title: Map layers
docs.text:
A layer switcher button (stacked-layers icon, bottom-left) lets you choose between two base maps. Below them, it lists your own map layers under "Your maps" (see Custom map overlays and Map files of places) and the Wikidata buildings layer under "External", each of which can be switched on and off.

The labels of both base maps are shown in the language you selected in Gramps Web, where the map data has a name in that language, and in the local name otherwise.

docs.title: Base Map
docs.text: The default layer, powered by OpenFreeMap (Liberty style for light mode, dark style for dark mode). This is a modern general-purpose map suitable for locating places.

docs.title: Historical Map
docs.text:
Switches the base map to OpenHistoricalMap (OHM), a community-driven project that maps the world as it existed at different points in time – think of it as a historical counterpart to OpenStreetMap.

When the Historical Map layer is active, the time slider also filters the map tiles themselves: OHM renders the map as it appeared in the selected year, so historical borders, place names, and features are shown instead of the modern ones. This makes it possible to see both your ancestor's location and the contemporary geographic and political context in a single view.

Note

OpenHistoricalMap coverage varies by region and period. Areas or eras with sparse contributions may show limited historical detail. If you notice missing or inaccurate historical data, consider contributing to OpenHistoricalMap – it is an open community project that anyone can edit.

docs.title: Custom map overlays
docs.text: In addition to the built-in base layers, you can turn any scanned historical map image – stored in Gramps as a Media object – into a custom overlay positioned on the live map. This is useful for scans of old city plans, parish maps, or property maps that you want to compare directly against modern or historical geography.

docs.title: Georeferencing an image
docs.text:
1. Open the media object for the scanned map image and switch to edit mode.
  2. Open the "Map" tab and click Edit coordinates. This opens a georeferencing dialog with the image alongside a map.
  3. Click Select a point on the map, then click the location on the map that a point on the image should correspond to. The image is placed on the map for the first time as soon as a point is selected.
  4. Use the Scale slider to resize the image and the Opacity slider to see the base map through it while positioning.
  5. Click Align the image and click on the map again to shift the image so that the pinned point lines up precisely.
  6. Repeat the scale, opacity, and align steps until the image matches the underlying geography, then save.

Behind the scenes, this stores the image's corner coordinates in a map:bounds attribute on the media object.

docs.title: Viewing overlays on the Map page
docs.text:
Once a media object has been georeferenced this way, it automatically becomes available as a toggleable layer on the Map page. Open the layer switcher (stacked-layers icon, bottom-left) to show or hide each overlay independently of the base map. Overlays are listed by the media object's title.

Each overlay has an opacity slider below its name, so you can see the base map through it.

docs.title: Map files of places
docs.text:
Places can have map files attached as media objects – for example the boundaries of a parish, a district, or an estate, or a route. Supported are KML (.kml), GeoJSON (.geojson), and GPX (.gpx) files.

When you select a place on the map, its map files are drawn on top of the map, using the colours stored in the file where it has them. This also works for places without coordinates: the map then zooms to the area covered by the files. While the place is selected, its files are listed in the layer switcher under "Your maps", where you can switch each of them off.

To add a map file to a place, add it to the place's gallery like any other media file.

docs.title: Wikidata buildings
docs.text:
The "Wikidata buildings" layer shows buildings recorded in Wikidata, such as churches, farms, or town houses. It is off by default and can be switched on in the layer switcher under "External". Buildings are only shown when the map is zoomed in far enough. When the time slider is active, only buildings that existed at the selected time are shown.

Click a building to see its details from Wikidata, such as when it was built or demolished, its addresses, occupants, and owners.

docs.title: Saving a building as a place
docs.text:
Users who can add objects see a Save as place button in the building's details. It opens the form for a new place, prefilled with the building's name in your language, a place type (Farm for farms, otherwise Building), its coordinates, and a link to the Wikidata item. Complete the form, for example by selecting the enclosing place, and save it.

If a place in your tree is at the same location as the building, the button reads Open saved place instead and shows that place.

Info

The server administrator can remove the Wikidata buildings layer with the mapWikidata option of the frontend configuration.

docs.title: Add media files
docs.text: There are two ways to add a new media file (an image, audio file, video file, or any other file), and existing media files can be linked to new objects as they are created:

docs.title: Add a new standalone media file
docs.text:
To add a standalone media file, click the + icon in the top app bar and select "Media Object".

Click on "select a file" to select a file from your computer. On a mobile device, clicking this button will give you the option of directly taking a photo with your device's camera.

Optionally,

  • enter a description of the media file under "title"
  • enter a date
  • set the media file as private (which will make it visible only to users with sufficient authorization)

Click "add" to upload the file and create the media object.

docs.title: Add a new media file and link it to another object
docs.text:
The following object types in Gramps can have media objects attached: people, families, events, places, sources, and citations.

In the detail view of any object, click the blue edit button in the bottom right (if you do not see it, your user does not have edit permissions). Click on the "gallery" tab and click the blue + button.

A dialog will open that offers the same fields as described in the previous section. Click "save" to upload the file, add a new media object, and link it to the viewed object.

docs.title: Profile pictures
docs.text: The first image in a person's gallery is used as their profile picture. In edit mode, it is marked with a "Profile picture" badge. To use a different image, move it to the first position with the arrow buttons on the gallery thumbnails, or drag it there: with the mouse, press the thumbnail and move it; on a touch screen, press and hold it until it is picked up. If a person has no media yet, edit mode shows an Add profile picture placeholder instead. Click it to upload a new media file or select an existing one.

docs.title: Link existing media files when creating an object
docs.text:
When you create a new person, family, event, place, source or citation, the form has a "Media" section. There you can select one or more existing media objects, which are linked to the new object when you save it.

When you create a person together with their birth and death events, the selected media objects are linked to the person only, not to the events.

docs.title: Browsing media
docs.text:
The media view shows the media objects as a gallery of thumbnails or as a list; the choice is remembered in your browser. Like the other list views, it can be sorted (including by date), filtered and used to select and delete media in bulk.

Clicking a tile in the gallery opens the media in the lightbox. Use the arrow keys, swipe, or click the arrow buttons to step through the filtered and sorted results, across pages. The Details button in the lightbox opens the media object's page. Clicking a row in the list layout opens the media object's page directly.

Videos are shown with a thumbnail and a play button. Audio and video files can be played on the media object's page, in the lightbox, in blog posts and when embedded in notes.

docs.title: Text recognition (OCR)
docs.text:
If the server administrator has enabled OCR support, a "Text Recognition" button appears below the image in a media object's detail view.

Click "Text Recognition", choose the language of the text shown in the image, then click "Run". The image is processed with Tesseract OCR and the recognized text is displayed below.

If your user has edit permissions, click "Save as Note" to create a new note (of type "Transcript") containing the recognized text and link it to the media object.

Tip

OCR accuracy depends heavily on image quality and the selected language. If the result looks wrong, try a different language – for example, historical German documents often need the Fraktur variant rather than plain German.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The bell in the top app bar opens the notifications. A badge on the bell shows the number of unread notifications. The menu lists running tasks and the latest notifications; Show all opens the full notification log. On small screens, the bell opens the log directly.

Notifications are about:

  • Changes by other users. When other users change the tree while you are using Gramps Web, a notification says who changed what, e.g. "Edit Person" or "12 changes". Click it to open the change in the revision history. Changes that have no Gramps Web user, such as changes made directly to a shared database with Gramps Desktop, are shown without a name. This is only available to users who can see the revision history (members and above).
  • Background tasks – such as imports and exports, generating reports, OCR text recognition, database upgrades, deleting or editing many objects, and search index rebuilds – showing their state (e.g. pending, started, in progress) and notifying you when they complete or fail.
  • Errors that occurred during your session – failed API requests, background task errors, save failures, or browser-level errors.

Finished exports and media archives can be downloaded from their notification, also after you have left the Export page.

Some notifications include structured detail, such as the error message of a failed task. Clicking such an entry in the notification log opens a dialog with a breakdown of the error data and a Copy JSON button. This is useful when reporting a bug, as the JSON contains the exact error information from the server.

Use Clear All in the notification log to dismiss all notifications.

Tasks that change the whole tree, such as an import, a restore, deleting all objects, or rebuilding the search index, cannot run at the same time. If you start one while another is running, a message says that another task is already running on this tree, and the running task is shown with its progress.

Note

Notifications are stored in memory only and are cleared when you reload the page. Gramps Web checks for changes by other users only while it is open, so changes made while you were away are not reported; see Revision history for those.

docs.title: Private records
docs.text: Any record in the tree can be marked as private. Together with the user roles, this decides who sees what.

docs.title: Who can see what
docs.text:
Gramps Web is never open to the public: only users with an account can see anything. "Public" in Gramps simply means "not private", i.e. visible to every logged-in user of the tree.

Role Public records Private records Guest view – Member view view Contributor view, add view, add Editor, Owner, Administrator view, add, edit, delete view, add, edit, delete

For guests, private records don't exist: they are left out of pages, lists, search results, charts, reports, exports, and AI assistant answers. This is enforced where the server reads the database, not by hiding things in the app, so a guest cannot get to private data in any other way either.

Accounts that have not been approved yet (after self-registration) cannot log in at all.

So if relatives or other people with a guest account should not see certain information, mark it as private. If all users of a tree may see everything, give them the member role (or higher) and there is no need to mark anything as private.

docs.title: Living people are not private automatically
docs.text:
Nothing is made private automatically – not even people who are still alive. Data of living people is visible to guests until you mark it as private. This also applies to imported trees.

To make the people who are probably alive private in Gramps Web:

  1. In the people list, open the advanced filter and add the condition "People probably alive" (leave the date empty for today). Apply the filter.
  2. Click Select, tick the checkbox in the header, and choose Select All.
  3. Choose the Privacy action and mark the records as private.

"Probably alive" is estimated from the dates of the person and their relatives. People without any usable dates are considered alive. Check the result, and keep in mind that the estimate can change as you add data.

Marking a person as private hides the person, but not their events, notes, media, or families – see below. Gramps Desktop has more tools to set the privacy of many related records at once, which you can use with the Sync addon.

People who die later don't become public automatically either. Whether you want that is up to you – many researchers prefer to keep collected information private for some time.

docs.title: Reading the lock icons
docs.text:
Users who can view private data see a lock next to private items. There are two kinds:

  • Filled lock – the record itself is private. On a person's page, for example, a filled lock next to an event means the event is private, and next to a child that the child is private.
  • Outline lock – only the link is private, not the record it leads to. For example, a person's link to an event can be private while the event itself is public. The event is then hidden from that person's page but still visible elsewhere, such as on the pages of other participants or in the event list.

If both the record and its link are private, the filled lock is shown.

The same distinction applies to children (the child or the child's link to the family), associations, repository links of a source, and media in a gallery. Names, attributes, addresses, and URLs belong to their record and only have the filled lock.

docs.title: Making something private
docs.text:
You need edit permissions to change privacy.

  • A whole record: open its page, enter edit mode, and click the lock button in the toolbar.
  • Part of a record – an alternate name, attribute, address, URL, association, child link, or repository link: open the edit dialog of that item and turn on the Private switch. The primary name has no switch, since the person would otherwise show as "Private".
  • An event from a person's or family's page: the event's edit dialog has a privacy switch for the event itself. If the event is shared with other people, it only becomes editable after Edit for everyone, since it is private for all of them.
  • A person's link to an event: on the event page, open the participant's row in edit mode. The privacy switch there applies only to that participant's link, so the event stays visible for the other participants.
  • A media object in a gallery: in edit mode, click the lock in the corner of the tile.
  • Many records at once: select them in a list and use the Privacy action, see Lists.

To check which records in a list are private, turn on the Privacy column in the column picker of the list.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Making a record private does not make the records it links to private. If a person is private, their events, the families they belong to, and the notes attached to them are still visible unless they are private themselves. Use the advanced filter or the Privacy column to check related records.
  • Making a family or event private hides it, but not the people in it.
  • DNA matches and Y-DNA data have their own Private switch in their dialogs.
  • Exports and media archives made by a user who cannot view private data contain no private records or files.
  • Privacy is a Gramps feature, so records marked as private in Gramps Desktop are private in Gramps Web as well, and vice versa.

docs.title: Recently Browsed Objects
docs.text:
History in the sidebar opens the Recently Browsed Objects page, which lists the last objects you opened in Gramps Web, with the most recently viewed at the top. Up to 20 objects are remembered.

This is useful for quickly navigating back to a person, family, or other object you were looking at earlier in your session, without having to search for it again.

Click any entry to go back to that object. Use the Clear All button to reset the list.

The history is stored in the browser's local storage – it is specific to the current device and browser, and is not shared with other users.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
In a single-tree installation, anybody can register a new account at a Gramps Web instance, but it will need to be enabled manually by a site owner before it can be used to log in.

In a multi-tree installation, users additionally require the tree ID to sign up; in practice, this means they can sign up using a registration link shared by the tree owner.

docs.title: 1. Find registration form
docs.text:
On the login form on the home page of Gramps Web, usually there is a link "Register new account".

If this link is missing, either registration is disabled on this server, or it is a multi-tree installation of Gramps Web. In either case, contact the tree owner, who can create an account for you or send you a registration link.

If the server supports signing in with an external account (such as Google, Microsoft, or your organization's single sign-on), the registration page offers these as well. Choosing one creates your account without a password and without the e-mail confirmation below. Unless the server assigns roles automatically, the account still has to be enabled by the tree owner (step 4).

The tree owner can find and copy the registration link under Settings/Administration.

docs.title: 2. Submit registration form
docs.text: The registration form has four mandatory fields: username, password, e-mail address, and full name. When all four fields have been filled, click "submit" to start the registration process.

docs.title: 3. Confirm e-mail address
docs.text:
After the form has been submitted, an automated e-mail will be sent to the e-mail address provided containing an e-mail confirmation link. Clicking it will open a confirmation page.

If the confirmation e-mail does not arrive (and you have checked your Spam folder), it could be that e-mail has not been configured correctly by the Gramps Web server administrator.

docs.title: 4. Enable account
docs.text:
After the e-mail address has been confirmed, the tree owner will receive an e-mail notification and can enable the new user account by going to the "User administration" section in settings page (accessible via the user icon in the top app bar) and changing the user role from "disabled" to any of the other roles.

Note that the new user will not receive an automated notification that their account has been enabled, so it is advisible for the administrator to notify them personally.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
A report is a formatted, downloadable document generated from your family tree data. Reports are the same plugins available in Gramps Desktop – see the Gramps Wiki page on Reports for a full overview. The web interface runs the same report engine on the server and delivers the resulting file to your browser.

Reports are accessible from the sidebar.

docs.title: Report categories
docs.text:
The Reports page lists all available reports grouped by category:

  • Text Reports – narrative or tabular documents such as ancestor lists, descendant reports, and birthday calendars. Output formats include PDF, ODT/OpenDocument, RTF, HTML, and others.
  • Graphical Reports – charts and diagrams such as ancestor trees and fan charts. Output formats include PDF, SVG, PNG, and others.
  • Trees – family tree diagrams.
  • Books – multi-chapter report books that combine several text and graphical reports into a single document.
  • Web Pages – static website generators that produce a complete set of HTML pages from your tree.

The reports shown depend on which Gramps report plugins are installed on the server.

docs.title: Running a report
docs.text:
Click a report to open its options page, which shows:

  • Description – what the report contains
  • Author and Version of the plugin
  • Options – report-specific settings such as the starting person, number of generations, output format, page size, and other parameters

Adjust the options as needed, then click Generate. The report is generated on the server and the resulting file is downloaded to your browser automatically.

Tip

Most reports default to the database home person – the home person set in the Gramps database, which may differ from your personal home person setting in the browser. If the report covers the wrong person, change the person option in the report's settings.

docs.title: Revision History
docs.text:
The revision history view shows all edits that have been made to the family tree.

The list view shows the edits grouped by "transactions". A transaction is a group of one or more additions, deletions, or changes to Gramps objects. For instance, adding a new family with two existing persons as father and mother generates a transaction with one added family object and two modified person objects (because they contain the link to the new family object).

Clicking on a transaction opens the transaction detail view. It contains the list of individual additions, deletions, and updates by Gramps object.

Selecting an individual change opens a view of the raw JSON representation of the Gramps object with additions and deletions highlighted in green and red, respectively. A button above the diff takes you straight to the object's own page.

docs.title: Revisions of a single object
docs.text:
To see the history of one particular person, family, event, or other object, open its page and switch to the Revisions tab. It lists every change made to that object, newest first, with the type of change (added, updated, or deleted), the user who made it, and when. Clicking an entry opens the transaction it belongs to, where you can inspect the diff or undo it.

Click Show more to load older entries; for objects with a very long history, only the most recent revisions are shown. For objects last changed before the revision history was recorded, the tab only shows the time of the last change.

Note

The Revisions tab is visible to members and above and requires Gramps Web API version 3.22 or later.

docs.title: Undoing a revision
docs.text:
On the transaction detail page, an Undo button allows you to reverse that transaction. Clicking it checks whether the undo can be performed cleanly.

Clean undo – if none of the objects affected by the transaction have been modified since, the undo can proceed without risk. A confirmation dialog is shown and clicking Undo reverses the transaction.

Force required – if one or more affected objects have been modified by a later transaction, a clean undo is not possible. The dialog warns that forcing the undo may result in data inconsistencies, since later changes that depend on the objects in question will be preserved as-is even though the underlying objects are being reverted. You can then either cancel or click Force undo to proceed anyway.

In both cases the undo runs as a background task and a progress indicator is shown.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: The search page is accessible by clicking the magnifying glass icon in the top app bar, or by pressing the s keyboard shortcut.

docs.title: Full-text search
docs.text:
Type a query into the search field. Results appear as you type, from the second character on; press Enter to search for a single character. Gramps Web searches across all object types – people, families, events, places, sources, citations, repositories, notes, and media – and returns matching results ranked by relevance. To clear the search, click the clear button in the field or press Escape.

Each result shows the object type, its name, and some details, for example the birth and death of a person, the marriage of a family, the author of a source, or the first line of a note. Click any result to open the corresponding detail page.

docs.title: Search syntax
docs.text:
• All words must match. Müller Berlin finds objects that contain both words.
  • or finds objects that contain either word, e.g. Meyer or Maier. and can be typed between words too, but it makes no difference.
  • or applies to the words directly next to it: Meyer or Maier Berlin means "(Meyer or Maier) and Berlin". Parentheses are not supported.
  • Quotes match a phrase, i.e. words in this order: "Johann Georg".
  • Wildcard: a trailing * matches any ending, e.g. Mey* matches "Meyer", "Meyers", "Meyerhofer", etc. This also works for phrases: "Johann Georg"*.
  • The last word is completed. If the query ends in a letter or digit, it is searched as if it ended in *, so Anna Smi already finds "Anna Smith". To search for the last word exactly, end the query with a space, or put the word in quotes. The same applies to the search boxes of the object selectors and the map.
  • or and and are recognized in any case. To search for one of these words itself, put it in quotes.
  • Words cannot be excluded; there is no "not".

docs.title: What the search finds
docs.text:
• Accents don't need to match: "Müller" also finds "Muller", and "muller" finds "Müller".
  • Families and events are also found by the names of their people, e.g. "Müller" finds the families and events of everyone named Müller. These results are ranked below direct matches.
  • Standard types are found by their names in your interface language, e.g. "Taufe" finds baptisms in the German interface.
  • Underscores separate words, so "microfilm" finds a media file named scanned_microfilm.png.
  • Users who can't view private records don't find objects through private information, such as a family through the name of a private member.

docs.title: Filtering by object type
docs.text: Below the search field, toggle buttons for each object type (People, Families, Events, Places, …) let you narrow results to one or more specific types. By default all types are searched. Activating one or more toggles restricts results to those types only.

docs.title: User Settings
docs.text:
User Settings are accessible via the user icon in the top app bar, then User Settings. The page is organized into collapsible sections. Changes take effect immediately unless noted otherwise.

Note

Changes in User Settings only affect your own account. Settings that affect all users of the tree are managed in Administration Settings.

docs.title: Account
docs.text: Covers your profile information, credentials, and account security.

docs.title: User information
docs.text: Shows your username and current user role (e.g. Guest, Member, Editor). These are read-only.

docs.title: Change e-mail
docs.text: Enter a new e-mail address and click Submit to update the address associated with your account. The e-mail address is used for password resets and (if configured) notifications.

docs.title: Change password
docs.text:
Enter your current password and a new password, then click Submit. You stay signed in on the current device, while your sessions on other devices and browsers end within 15 minutes. If you have forgotten your current password, use the Forgot password link on the login page instead.

This section is hidden if the server only allows signing in through an external provider (see OIDC authentication).

docs.title: Linked sign-in methods
docs.text:
If your server offers single sign-on (see OIDC authentication), you can link an account from a provider, such as Google or your organization's login, to your Gramps Web account. You can then sign in with that provider and land in your existing account, with your role and your edits. This section only appears when single sign-on is enabled and the server supports linking (Gramps Web API 3.24 and later).

To link an account, click Link with and the provider's name, sign in at the provider, and you are taken back to your settings. If you haven't signed in recently, you are asked to sign in again first.

A provider account can only be linked to one Gramps Web account. If you see "This sign-in is already linked to another account", it is linked elsewhere, for example to an account that was created when you first signed in with that provider. An administrator can delete that other account, after which you can link it to yours.

To unlink an account, click Unlink. If it is your last linked sign-in method, you also need to enter your password, so that you can still sign in afterwards. If your account was created through single sign-on and you never set a password, use Forgot password on the login page to set one first (this needs the server to send e-mails). If the server only allows signing in through a provider, the last linked account can't be unlinked.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Controls display preferences saved on your device.

docs.title: Language
docs.text: Select the language for the Gramps Web interface. The language setting is stored in the browser's local storage and applies only to the current device.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text:
Choose between:

  • System – follows the operating system's light/dark preference (default)
  • Light – always use the light theme
  • Dark – always use the dark theme

The theme setting is stored in the browser's local storage.

docs.title: Default family tree view
docs.text:
Sets which chart type opens by default when you navigate to the Family Tree page. Options are Ancestor Tree, Descendant Tree, Hourglass Graph, Relationship Graph, and Fan Chart.

This preference is stored in the browser's local storage.

docs.title: API token
docs.text:
Copies your current session token to the clipboard. The token can be used to authenticate directly against the REST API, for example in the interactive Swagger UI served by your Gramps Web instance at /api/swagger-ui.

Click Launch Swagger to open the Swagger UI in a new tab with your session already available.

Note

The session token is short-lived. Copy it immediately before using it in Swagger, as it may expire.

docs.title: Using Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
Keyboard shortcuts allow you to navigate quickly through Gramps Web without using your mouse, saving you clicks and time.

From any view, you can jump directly to common actions and pages with just a few keystrokes. For example, press s on your keyboard to open the search, g + c to navigate to the Family Tree, or n + p to create a new person.

To see a complete list of all available keyboard shortcuts, simply press ? at any time.

docs.title: Start a new tree
docs.text:
This page walks you through the first steps in an empty family tree: adding yourself, adding your parents, and seeing the result in the family tree chart. It takes about 15 minutes.

If you already have a family tree in another genealogy program or in Gramps Desktop, you don't need to enter it again by hand – see Import data instead.

Note

Adding people requires the Editor role or higher. The owner of a tree always has it. See User system for all roles.

docs.title: 1. Create a place
docs.text:
In Gramps, a place is created once and then selected for every event that happened there – for example the births of several siblings in the same town. This is why a place has to exist before you can select it as someone's place of birth.

To create the place where you were born:

  1. Click the + (Add) button in the top app bar and choose Place.
  2. Enter the Name of the place, and optionally its Type (such as city or village).
  3. Optionally, click Pick on map to set its coordinates, so the place appears on the map.
  4. Click Add.

Create the birth places of your parents in the same way. If you don't know a place yet, skip it – you can add it later.

docs.title: 2. Add yourself
docs.text:
Go back to the home page. While the tree is empty, it shows a Get started card. Click New Person to open the form for a new person:

  • Name – your given name and surname
  • Gender
  • Birth Date – see Entering dates below
  • Birth Place – click Select an existing place and search for the place you created

Leave the death fields empty and click Add. The page of the new person opens.

The first person created in an empty tree automatically becomes your Home Person: the person the family tree chart starts from. You can choose a different Home Person at any time on the home page.

docs.title: Entering dates
docs.text: A date is entered as separate year, month, and day fields. If you only know the year, fill in only the year. For uncertain dates, change the date's type – for example to "about" or "before" – instead of guessing an exact day.

docs.title: 3. Add your parents
docs.text:
1. Click Family Tree in the sidebar. The chart shows you as the Home Person.
  2. Click the pencil button in the bottom right corner to switch on edit mode.
  3. Click the small + button on your card. The Add Family Member dialog opens.
  4. Next to Father, click the + icon to create a new person, fill in the form as before, and save. Your father appears in the chart, already linked to you.
  5. Repeat with Mother.

The link icon next to each relationship connects a person who already exists in your tree instead of creating a new one.

In the same way, click the + on any card in the chart to add that person's parents, children, or spouse. Each change is saved immediately. To leave edit mode, click the close button in the top app bar.

docs.title: 4. See the result
docs.text: The chart now shows you with your parents. Try the other chart types in the tabs at the top of the page – for example the Fan Chart – and click any person's card to centre the chart on them. See Family Tree for all charts and options.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Understand the structure. See How Gramps organizes data for how people, families, events, places, and sources fit together.
  • Add more details. Open a person's page – for example with the Person Details button in the chart toolbar – to add further events, notes, sources, and more. See Editing in the tree view for what can be done directly in the chart.
  • Add photos and documents. See Add media files.
  • Invite your family. Relatives need their own account on your tree; see Manage users and Registration.

docs.title: Tag people in photos
docs.text:
Gramps Web allows tagging people in photographs, similar to Gramps Desktop, linking the person and the media object. This is simplified by automated face detection.

A region of an image can be linked not only to a person, but also to a family, event, place, source or citation – for example a building in a photo, or a citation on a scanned page. An object can have several regions in the same image, for instance on an album page with more than one photo of the same person.

docs.title: Linking a region
docs.text:
To link a region of an image to an object, follow these steps:

  • Open the detail view of the media object, e.g. by clicking on "show details" in the full-screen preview.
  • Click the blue edit button in the bottom-right corner. If you do not see this button, your user does not have edit permissions.
  • Overlayed on the image, you will see boxes with dashed border corresponding to detected faces. Click on a box to select it.
  • To draw a region yourself instead, click the button and drag a rectangle over the image. Drawing also works on touch screens.
  • Click the "Link" button and select an existing person, family, event, place, source or citation.

Linked regions are shown with a solid border and a label with the name of the linked object and the icon of its type. In the full-screen view of the image, clicking a linked region opens the linked object.

docs.title: Editing a region
docs.text:
In edit mode, click a linked region to select it. Then you can:

  • move it by dragging it, or resize it with its four corner handles. The change is saved when you release the mouse button or lift your finger.
